items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "albedo".
items.answer: The fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student in Nairobi is checking notes on black-body radiation, emissivity and albedo. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Water vapour responds to temperature as a feedback; CO₂ is a long-lived forcing that sets the temperature and hence the amount of water vapour.
Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water; sea-level rise comes mainly from thermal expansion and melting of land ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctica).
Only hot objects emit black-body radiation.
N₂, O₂ and Ar, which make up 99 % of dry air, absorb almost no infrared; only molecules whose vibrations change their dipole moment are greenhouse gases.
items.answer: Only hot objects emit black-body radiation.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: All objects above 0 K emit; Earth at about 288 K emits mainly in the infrared around 10 μm.

items.stem: Sunlight of intensity 950 W m⁻² falls perpendicularly on grassland with albedo 0.25. Calculate the intensity absorbed.
items.answer: 712 W m⁻²
items.markingKey: Absorbed = (1 − α)I (M1) = 712 W m⁻² (A1).

items.stem: A surface at 310 K radiates 300 W per square metre. Determine its emissivity.

This question is about black-body radiation, emissivity and albedo.

(a) A satellite measures 800 W m⁻² of sunlight incident on a region near Toronto and 240 W m⁻² scattered back to space. Calculate the albedo of the region. [2]

(b) Explain the difference between albedo and emissivity. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Painting city roofs white is an effective way to combat global warming." [4]
items.answer: (a) 0.300 (b) Emissivity describes how well a surface emits radiation compared with a black body at the same temperature; albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects. (c) White roofs are a useful local adaptation that lowers building temperatures, but on their own they make only a small contribution to tackling global warming.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] α = scattered/incident (M1) = 240/800 = 0.300 (A1). (b) [4 marks] Emissivity describes how well a surface emits radiation compared with a black body at the same temperature; albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects. (c) [4 marks] For: raises the local albedo, reducing absorbed sunlight and urban heat island effects; cheap and immediate. Against: global effect is small because roofs are a tiny fraction of Earth’s area; can increase heating demand in winter; does not address CO₂ emissions. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: White roofs are a useful local adaptation that lowers building temperatures, but on their own they make only a small contribution to tackling global warming.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power"?
items.answer: albedo

items.stem: Briefly explain why Earth’s albedo varies from day to day.
items.answer: Albedo depends on cloud cover, snow and ice cover, vegetation and the angle of incidence of sunlight, all of which change with weather and season.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Albedo depends on cloud cover, snow and ice cover, vegetation and the angle of incidence of sunlight, all of which change with weather and season. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A planet with albedo 0 absorbs no radiation." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Albedo 0 means nothing is reflected, so all incident radiation is absorbed.
items.markingKey: Albedo 0 means nothing is reflected, so all incident radiation is absorbed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A solar thermal collector of area 2.5 m² receives sunlight of intensity 800 W m⁻². Its surface has albedo 0.08 and emissivity 0.10 (a selective coating). (a) Calculate the power absorbed. (b) The plate reaches 360 K; calculate the power it radiates. (c) Explain why a low emissivity coating is chosen. (d) Determine the maximum power available to heat water if the surroundings are at 290 K (net radiation only).
items.answer: (a) 0.92 × 800 × 2.5 = 1840 W; (b) 0.10 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 2.5 × 360⁴ = 238 W; (c) it absorbs visible light well but emits little infrared, so less energy is lost; (d) net loss = eσA(360⁴ − 290⁴) = 138 W, leaving ≈ 1.70 kW.

items.stem: Taking the solar constant as 1360 W m⁻² and Earth’s albedo as 0.25, calculate the equilibrium temperature of Earth with no greenhouse effect.

In a simple model, Earth’s surface temperature is proportional to the fourth root of the absorbed solar power. If the absorbed power changes by a factor of 0.98, calculate the new surface temperature, starting from 288 K.

A computer model calculates the equilibrium temperature T of a rocky planet with no atmosphere placed at different distances d from the Sun (solar constant 1360 W m⁻² at 1 AU). Theory: σT⁴ = (1 − α)S/(4d²), so T⁴ ∝ 1/d².

d / AU | T / K
0.40 | 395
0.70 | 301
1.00 | 249
1.50 | 207
2.00 | 178
3.00 | 145

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the albedo α of the planet. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State α with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) T⁴ (y) against 1/d² (x); (b) gradient ≈ 3.89 × 10⁹ K⁴ AU²; (c) 0.351; (d) 0.35 ± 0.01
items.markingKey: (a) T⁴ (y) against 1/d² (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 3.89 × 10⁹ K⁴ AU² – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) α = 1 − 4σ × gradient/S = 0.351 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 0.01; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about energy balance of the Earth-atmosphere system.

(a) In a simple model, Earth’s surface temperature is proportional to the fourth root of the absorbed solar power. If the absorbed power changes by a factor of 0.98, calculate the new surface temperature, starting from 288 K. [2]

(b) Distinguish between the solar constant and the mean incident intensity at the top of the atmosphere. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "A zero-dimensional energy-balance model is too simple to be useful in climate science." [4]
items.answer: (a) 286.5 K (b) The solar constant (~1360 W m⁻²) is measured perpendicular to the rays; the mean over the whole surface and over day and night is a quarter of this (~340 W m⁻²). (c) Simple models are valuable for understanding and estimates, but detailed predictions require complex general circulation models (NOS: role of models).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] T ∝ P^¼ (M1); T = 288 × 0.98^¼ = 286.5 K (A1). (b) [4 marks] The solar constant (~1360 W m⁻²) is measured perpendicular to the rays; the mean over the whole surface and over day and night is a quarter of this (~340 W m⁻²). (c) [4 marks] For: ignores latitude, oceans, clouds and feedbacks; cannot predict regional changes. Against: captures the key physics of energy in = energy out; gives correct order of magnitude (255 K vs 288 K) and shows the role of albedo and greenhouse gases; used to check complex models. items.stem: Briefly explain why water vapour is considered a feedback rather than a driver of climate change.
items.answer: Its concentration is controlled by temperature (evaporation and condensation within days); warming caused by CO₂ increases water vapour, which amplifies the warming.

(b) Explain, at the molecular level, how carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "The greenhouse effect is harmful to life on Earth." [4]
items.answer: (a) 9.06 × 10⁻⁶ m (b) The bending and asymmetric stretching vibrations of CO₂ change its dipole moment; when the frequency of infrared radiation matches a natural vibration frequency (resonance), the photon is absorbed and the molecule vibrates more strongly, later re-emitting IR in a random direction. items.stem: Explain why reducing emissions today will not stop warming immediately.
items.answer: CO₂ stays in the atmosphere for centuries and the oceans have a large heat capacity, so the climate responds slowly; temperatures continue to rise until a new energy balance is reached.

items.stem: A teacher in Dubai asks a class to choose the one correct statement about enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change. Which statement should be chosen?
options: All gases in the atmosphere are greenhouse gases.
Greenhouse gases trap heat like the glass of a greenhouse prevents convection.
A planet with albedo 0 absorbs no radiation.
Water vapour responds to temperature as a feedback; CO₂ is a long-lived forcing that sets the temperature and hence the amount of water vapour.
items.answer: Water vapour responds to temperature as a feedback; CO₂ is a long-lived forcing that sets the temperature and hence the amount of water vapour.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Water vapour responds to temperature as a feedback; CO₂ is a long-lived forcing that sets the temperature and hence the amount of water vapour.

items.stem: In a simple model, the radiative forcing from CO₂ is ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C₀) W m⁻² and the equilibrium warming is ΔT = λΔF with λ = 0.80 K W⁻¹ m². (a) Calculate ΔF and ΔT for a rise from 280 ppm to 420 ppm. (b) Calculate the forcing for a doubling of CO₂ and hence the climate sensitivity. (c) Explain why the observed warming to date (≈ 1.2 K) is less than the answer to (a). (d) Discuss one source of uncertainty in λ.
items.answer: (a) ΔF = 5.35 ln 1.5 = 2.17 W m⁻², ΔT = 1.7 K; (b) 5.35 ln 2 = 3.71 W m⁻², sensitivity ≈ 3.0 K; (c) oceans are still absorbing energy (thermal inertia) and aerosols have a cooling effect; (d) cloud feedbacks are poorly constrained.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "albedo"?
options: The continuous spectrum of electromagnetic radiation emitted by an ideal black body, whose shape depends only on temperature
A process that reduces the original change, such as increased infrared emission from a warmer surface
The solar constant divided by four (≈ 340 W m⁻²), because Earth intercepts sunlight over πR² but radiates over 4πR²
The fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power
items.answer: The fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power
items.markingKey: D. "albedo" is the fraction of incident radiation that is reflected (or scattered) by a surface or planet: total scattered power / total incident power.

items.stem: Why do N₂ and O₂ not act as greenhouse gases?
items.answer: Their symmetric vibrations do not change the molecular dipole moment, so they hardly absorb infrared

items.stem: Distinguish between mitigation and adaptation.

items.stem: Aiko is revising energy balance of the Earth-atmosphere system. Which of the following statements is correct?

Only hot objects emit black-body radiation.
A planet closer to the Sun must have a higher surface temperature.
Earth radiates infrared continuously, day and night, at a rate depending on its temperature.
items.answer: Earth radiates infrared continuously, day and night, at a rate depending on its temperature.

items.stem: Briefly explain why melting Arctic sea ice can accelerate warming.
items.answer: Ice has a high albedo and open ocean a low albedo; replacing ice with water means more solar radiation is absorbed, warming the region and melting more ice (positive feedback).

items.stem: Briefly explain why greenhouse gases warm the surface even though they re-emit the radiation they absorb.
items.answer: Re-emission is in all directions, so about half returns towards the surface; the surface receives extra infrared and must warm to restore energy balance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Re-emission is in all directions, so about half returns towards the surface; the surface receives extra infrared and must warm to restore energy balance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Freya.)

Real greenhouses work mainly by stopping convection; the atmospheric effect works by absorption and re-emission of infrared radiation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Clouds always cool the planet." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Clouds reflect sunlight (cooling) but also absorb and re-emit infrared (warming); the net effect depends on cloud type and height.

items.answer: Simple models are valuable for understanding and estimates, but detailed predictions require complex general circulation models (NOS: role of models).

items.stem:
This question is about black-body radiation, emissivity and albedo.

(a) A satellite measures 800 W m⁻² of sunlight incident on a region near Accra and 400 W m⁻² scattered back to space. Calculate the albedo of the region. [2]

(b) Distinguish between emissivity and albedo. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Painting city roofs white is an effective way to combat global warming." [4]
items.answer: (a) 0.500 (b) Emissivity describes how well a surface emits radiation compared with a black body at the same temperature; albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects. (c) White roofs are a useful local adaptation that lowers building temperatures, but on their own they make only a small contribution to tackling global warming.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] α = scattered/incident (M1) = 400/800 = 0.500 (A1). (b) [4 marks] Emissivity describes how well a surface emits radiation compared with a black body at the same temperature; albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects. (c) [4 marks] For: raises the local albedo, reducing absorbed sunlight and urban heat island effects; cheap and immediate. Against: global effect is small because roofs are a tiny fraction of Earth’s area; can increase heating demand in winter; does not address CO₂ emissions. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: White roofs are a useful local adaptation that lowers building temperatures, but on their own they make only a small contribution to tackling global warming.

(b) Explain the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect. [4]

items.answer: (a) 1.14 × 10⁻⁵ m (b) The natural greenhouse effect, from pre-industrial levels of water vapour and CO₂, keeps Earth about 33 K warmer than it would be otherwise; the enhanced effect is the additional warming caused by human emissions raising greenhouse gas concentrations. (c) The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life; it is the rapid human-driven enhancement that is harmful.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] λ = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T (M1) = 1.14 × 10⁻⁵ m (A1). Against: without the natural greenhouse effect Earth’s mean temperature would be about −18 °C; liquid oceans and life depend on it.
